result:
First large-scale empirical study of SKILL.md files. Its usable output is a 26-item catalog of "skill smells" plus a 13/44-level component taxonomy; the empirical findings are descriptive, not causal.

What you get:
- A rubric skeleton. 26 smells grouped by theme, of which 5 are static checks (word/char caps, backslash paths, XML in frontmatter description) and 21 need an LLM judge.
- A copyable judge design: per-smell definition, one positive and one negative example, binary answer, thinking mode. Reported weighted F1 0.78 on 53 hand-labeled files with a quantized Qwen3.6-27B.
- Prevalence numbers: 237 of 238 files have at least one smell, 10.5 on average, Rationalization Loophole in 94%. Smells rarely get removed once introduced.

What limits it: the "best practices" come from 29 web sources settled by majority vote, so the paper shows smells are common, not that they cause harm. Sample is popular public marketplace skills only. Detector metrics rest on 53 labeled files and one quantized open model.

Read it if you are building a skill linter or review rubric; the smell list and judge prompt format transfer directly. Skip the full text if you only want the catalog, since the note above already carries it. Read the methods section if you plan to reproduce or beat the 0.78 F1.
